entries.name: Discovery, identity & reputation
entries.title: How agents find and trust each other
entries.summary: Agent discovery and identity registries exist as drafts, but cross-ecosystem reputation is still nascent.
entries.reason:
The discovery and identity layer is where two agents establish who they are and whether they can be trusted before any commerce happens. Several registry and identity proposals are circulating, and a handful of reference implementations let agents publish verifiable identities and look one another up. The basic plumbing is real and improving quickly.

It earns an emerging color because the pieces do not yet interoperate across ecosystems. Reputation signals are siloed, identity standards are competing rather than converging, and there is no widely adopted way for an arbitrary agent to vet a counterparty it has never met. Until registries consolidate and reputation becomes portable, this layer is promising but not production-grade.

entries.name: Negotiation
entries.title: How agents agree on terms
entries.summary: Agent-to-agent negotiation protocols are early proposals with reference implementations but little real-world traffic.
entries.reason:
Negotiation covers the back-and-forth where two agents converge on the terms of a deal: price, scope, deadlines and obligations. A small number of protocols define message formats and negotiation flows, and demos exist showing agents exchanging structured offers. The conceptual model is sound and actively developed.

The color is experimental because almost none of this runs in production at scale. Negotiation today is mostly bespoke prompt-engineering inside individual agent frameworks rather than a shared, interoperable protocol. Standards are young, tooling is thin, and there is no broad agreement on how negotiated terms hand off to the contracts layer. It is a working prototype space, not a dependable foundation.

entries.name: Contracts & obligations
entries.title: How agreements become enforceable
entries.summary: On-chain delegation and obligation primitives are maturing, but agent-native contract authoring is still draft-stage.
entries.reason:
This layer turns a negotiated understanding into something enforceable: delegated permissions, encoded obligations, and the contract objects an AI jury can later evaluate. Delegation standards have working implementations and real wallet support, and obligation frameworks are being built out by several teams. The building blocks are concrete and improving.

It sits at emerging because the full path from a natural-language agreement to a deployed, machine-judgeable contract is not yet smooth. Obligation standards are still in draft, agent-native authoring tools are immature, and most deployments are pilots rather than load-bearing systems. The primitives are real; the end-to-end authoring experience is not yet there.

entries.name: Payment & escrow
entries.title: How value moves and is held
entries.summary: Stablecoin agent payments and escrow are shipping with real implementations and early production usage.
entries.reason:
Payment and escrow is the most mature commerce layer for agents today. Stablecoin rails are battle-tested, the HTTP 402 payment pattern has working libraries and live integrations, and on-chain escrow is a well-understood primitive that many teams ship. Agents can already pay one another and lock funds programmatically with off-the-shelf tools.

It earns an available color rather than full production because agent-specific payment protocols are still consolidating and end-to-end escrow tied to dispute resolution is only beginning to appear in real deployments. The money movement is solid; the agent-native conventions around it are still settling. Compared with every other layer, however, this is where you can actually transact today.

entries.name: Execution
entries.title: How agreed work actually gets done
entries.summary: Agent execution frameworks are fragmented and early; standardized, verifiable execution is largely unproven.
entries.reason:
Execution is where an agent performs the work it agreed to do — calling tools, running tasks, and producing the deliverable that will later be verified. A number of frameworks let agents execute actions, but they are vendor-specific and rarely designed for cross-agent, verifiable commerce. Each ecosystem reinvents its own execution loop.

The color is experimental because there is no shared, dependable standard for proving that contracted work was actually executed correctly. Most frameworks are young, naming and scope are unsettled, and the link between execution and verification is largely manual. It works in demos and inside single platforms, but not yet as interoperable commerce infrastructure.

entries.name: Verification & disputes
entries.title: How outcomes are judged and disputes resolved
entries.summary: AI-jury and oracle-based dispute resolution have live systems, but agent-native verification is still proving itself.
entries.reason:
Verification and disputes is where outcomes get judged: did the work meet the agreement, and if the parties disagree, who decides? Several real systems exist — optimistic oracles, decentralized arbitration courts, and AI-jury intelligent contracts — and some have processed real value on mainnet. This is a comparatively well-developed layer with shipping products.

It lands at emerging because agent-native dispute resolution at scale is still being proven. Existing arbitration systems were largely designed for human-driven disputes, and adapting them to high-volume, autonomous agent commerce is ongoing work. The infrastructure is real and improving, but the specific use case of agents routinely resolving disputes with one another is still early.

entries.name: ERC-7857
entries.title: Verifiable identity / agent identity NFTs
entries.summary: An early proposal for verifiable agent identity NFTs with limited reference implementation.
entries.reason:
ERC-7857 proposes a way to represent agent identity as verifiable, transferable on-chain objects, giving an agent a portable, cryptographically anchored sense of self. The idea fills a clear gap — agents need durable identities they can carry between platforms — and a reference implementation demonstrates the core mechanics.

It is graded experimental because the proposal is young and adoption is thin. There is little production usage, the surrounding tooling is minimal, and competing identity approaches mean it is far from a settled standard. It is a credible early proposal rather than something you would build a business on today.

entries.name: ERC-8004
entries.title: Trustless agent reputation/registry
entries.summary: A trustless agent registry/reputation standard with active development and early integrations.
entries.reason:
ERC-8004 aims to give agents a trustless registry and reputation layer, so a counterparty can be discovered and assessed without a central intermediary. The proposal has notable momentum, with active discussion and several teams experimenting with integrations, making it one of the more visible identity-layer efforts.

It sits at emerging because, while the spec is advancing and prototypes exist, it has not yet reached broad production deployment. Reputation data is still sparse and the network effects that make a registry valuable are only beginning to form. Promising and actively developed, but not yet something you can rely on across the ecosystem.

entries.name: A2A
entries.title: Google Agent-to-Agent negotiation protocol
entries.summary: Google's Agent-to-Agent protocol has strong backing and an open spec, with growing but early adoption.
entries.reason:
A2A is a protocol for agents to discover capabilities and exchange structured messages, backed by a major vendor and released as an open specification. That pedigree has driven real interest, a public spec, and a growing set of SDKs and demos showing agents coordinating across frameworks.

It is graded emerging because, despite the backing, real-world negotiation traffic over A2A is still limited and the protocol is evolving. It defines the messaging substrate well but leaves much of the actual negotiation logic to implementers, and production deployments doing genuine commercial negotiation are scarce. The foundation is strong; the usage is still ramping.

entries.name: ERC-7710
entries.title: Smart-contract delegation
entries.summary: A smart-contract delegation standard with finalized mechanics and real wallet/tooling support.
entries.reason:
ERC-7710 standardizes how one account can delegate scoped permissions to another via smart contracts, which is foundational for agents acting on a principal's behalf. The mechanics are well specified, multiple implementations exist, and it has meaningful support in wallet and delegation tooling already shipping to users.

It earns an available color because it is past the purely experimental stage and into early production: real applications use delegation for agent and account-abstraction flows. It stops short of the top score because agent-specific usage patterns are still maturing and broad, cross-wallet ubiquity has not fully arrived. Still, this is one of the more dependable primitives in the contracts layer.

entries.name: ERC-8183
entries.title: Obligations standard
entries.summary: A largely theoretical obligations standard; existence and exact scope need verification.
entries.reason:
ERC-8183 is listed as an obligations standard — a way to encode what each party owes under an agreement so it can be tracked and enforced. As mapped here it is closer to an idea than a shipping standard, with little public implementation evidence and an uncertain identifier.

It is graded theoretical and flagged for verification: the name and number may be a best-guess expansion, and Thread B should confirm whether this corresponds to a real proposal before grading it firmly. As a concept, obligation encoding is important and underdeveloped, which is exactly why it scores low today.
entries.notes: sample data — standard identity unverified; confirm ERC-8183 exists and adjust

entries.name: Arkhai
entries.title: Obligations / agreements framework
entries.summary: An obligations/agreements framework in early development, with limited public production usage.
entries.reason:
Arkhai is positioned as a framework for expressing agreements and obligations between parties in a machine-readable way, complementing on-chain contract primitives. There is an identifiable project and ecosystem presence, and the problem it targets — structured, enforceable agreements for agents — is squarely in the contracts layer.

It is graded experimental because public evidence of mature, production-scale deployments is limited. The framework appears to be in an early, actively developed phase rather than a settled, widely integrated standard. It is a credible effort in an important niche, but not yet proven infrastructure.

entries.name: x402
entries.title: HTTP 402 stablecoin payments
entries.summary: Revives HTTP 402 for stablecoin payments; spec is solid with working libraries and early production use.
entries.reason:
x402 revives the long-dormant HTTP 402 status code to let services charge for requests in stablecoins, making machine-to-machine payment a native part of the web request flow. It has a clear spec, working client and server libraries, and visible backing, and it slots neatly into how agents already make HTTP calls.

It earns an available color because real integrations exist and the developer experience is genuinely usable today, while broad production adoption is still building. The payment mechanics are dependable; what is still maturing is the surrounding ecosystem of facilitators, discovery and standardized pricing. Among agent payment approaches, x402 is one of the most ready to use right now.

entries.name: MPP
entries.title: Merchant/agent payment protocol
entries.summary: A merchant/agent payment protocol; identity is a best-guess and needs verification before firm grading.
entries.reason:
MPP is mapped here as a merchant- or agent-oriented payment protocol that would standardize how agents pay merchants for goods and services. The concept is reasonable and fits the payment layer, but the exact protocol behind this acronym is uncertain as listed.

It is graded experimental and flagged for verification: the expansion is a best-guess, and Thread B should confirm what MPP refers to and whether shipping implementations exist before assigning a confident score. As an early-stage payment protocol concept, a low-but-not-bottom score reflects genuine uncertainty rather than evidence of maturity.
entries.notes: sample data — acronym/identity unverified; confirm what MPP refers to

entries.name: APP
entries.title: Agent payments protocol
entries.summary: An agent payments protocol; acronym is a best-guess that needs verification before firm grading.
entries.reason:
APP is mapped as an agent payments protocol covering how autonomous agents initiate, authorize and settle payments among themselves. The category is real and increasingly important, and several efforts in the ecosystem aim at exactly this problem of programmatic agent payment authorization.

It is graded experimental and flagged for verification: the acronym is a best-guess and may collide with other named protocols, so Thread B should confirm the exact reference and its maturity. Pending that, a low score reflects the early state of standardized, interoperable agent payment authorization rather than the broader, more mature stablecoin rails it would sit on.
entries.notes: sample data — acronym/identity unverified; confirm what APP refers to

entries.name: OpenClaw
entries.title: Execution framework
entries.summary: An execution framework whose identity is unverified; treated as theoretical pending confirmation.
entries.reason:
OpenClaw is mapped as an execution framework for carrying out agreed agent work, but its identity is uncertain as listed and it may be a best-guess name. Execution frameworks in general are an active area, yet there is little public evidence tying this specific name to a mature, widely used project.

It is graded theoretical and explicitly flagged for verification: Thread B should determine whether OpenClaw is a real, shipping framework, what it actually does, and replace this placeholder accordingly. The low score reflects absence of confirmed evidence rather than a judgment that the underlying idea is unworkable.
entries.notes: sample data — name unverified; confirm whether OpenClaw exists

entries.name: Hermes
entries.title: Execution/messaging
entries.summary: An execution/messaging layer; the name is ambiguous and the specific reference needs verification.
entries.reason:
Hermes is mapped as an execution and messaging component for the agent stack. The name is widely reused across the industry (it attaches to oracles, messaging relays and other infrastructure), so the specific project intended here is ambiguous and needs confirmation.

It is graded experimental and flagged for verification: Thread B should pin down which Hermes is meant, what role it plays in agent execution, and grade that concrete project. The current score is a placeholder acknowledging that messaging/relay infrastructure exists and works in places, but the specific reference and its readiness for agent commerce are unconfirmed.
entries.notes: sample data — ambiguous name; confirm which Hermes is meant

entries.name: GenLayer
entries.title: Intelligent-contract AI jury
entries.summary: Intelligent contracts with an AI-validator jury; a live network powering real dispute resolution.
entries.reason:
GenLayer provides intelligent contracts whose validators act as an AI jury, able to evaluate natural-language statements and evidence to reach a verdict. It is the engine behind Internet Court, with a working network, an SDK, deployed contracts and a concrete dispute-resolution model that targets exactly the agent-commerce use case.

It earns an available color because it is genuinely usable today — contracts deploy and resolve — while still maturing toward heavy production volume. Graded without boosterism: the technology is real and shipping, but autonomous agents routinely resolving high-stakes disputes through it at scale is still an emerging practice rather than an everyday reality. Strong and load-bearing for this stack, with room to harden.

entries.name: Kleros
entries.title: Decentralized arbitration
entries.summary: A live decentralized arbitration court with years of real disputes, though human-centric by design.
entries.reason:
Kleros is a decentralized arbitration protocol that has been live for years, using crypto-economic incentives and juror voting to resolve disputes across a range of real applications. It has handled meaningful volumes of genuine cases and is one of the most battle-tested dispute-resolution systems in the space.

It earns an available color rather than the top score in the context of agent commerce specifically: its design centers on human jurors and human-readable disputes, so adapting it to high-volume, fully autonomous agent disputes is not its native mode. As proven dispute infrastructure it is mature; as agent-native verification it is solid but not purpose-built.

entries.name: UMA
entries.title: Optimistic oracle
entries.summary: A production optimistic oracle securing significant value and integrated across many protocols.
entries.reason:
UMA's optimistic oracle is a production system that lets protocols ask questions and resolve them through an assert-and-dispute mechanism backed by economic incentives. It secures significant value, is integrated by many well-known protocols, and has a long live track record of resolving real-world data requests on mainnet.

It earns a production color because it is dependable, widely adopted infrastructure that you can build on today. For agent commerce it provides a proven way to verify off-chain facts and outcomes, which is directly useful in the verification layer. Its main limitation for this stack is latency and the optimistic challenge window, not maturity — as oracle infrastructure it is among the most ready in the entire taxonomy.

entries.name: Discovery → Negotiation
entries.title: Found agents handing off into negotiation
entries.summary: Discovered agents can begin negotiating, but the handoff lacks a shared, standardized contract.
entries.reason:
This edge asks whether an agent that has just discovered a counterparty can smoothly move into negotiating terms with it. In practice the two steps are increasingly linked: discovery protocols expose capability descriptions that negotiation flows can consume, and some frameworks demonstrate a clean find-then-negotiate path.

It is graded emerging because the handoff is not yet standardized across ecosystems. Identity and discovery outputs do not map cleanly onto negotiation inputs in a vendor-neutral way, so most working examples live inside a single framework. The composition is real where one vendor owns both ends, but brittle across the open ecosystem.

entries.name: Negotiation → Contracts
entries.title: Negotiated terms becoming enforceable contracts
entries.summary: Turning negotiated terms into deployed, enforceable contracts is mostly manual and unstandardized.
entries.reason:
This integration covers whether the output of a negotiation can be turned directly into an enforceable contract object — delegated permissions, obligations and the statement a jury could later judge. Conceptually the pipeline is clear, and a few demos show negotiated terms being encoded on-chain.

It is graded experimental because in practice this step is largely manual and bespoke. There is no widely adopted schema that maps negotiated terms onto contract primitives automatically, so the handoff usually requires custom glue code per project. The two layers can be wired together, but not yet through a dependable, reusable standard.

entries.name: Contracts → Payment/Escrow
entries.title: Contracts triggering payment and escrow
entries.summary: Contracts can lock and release escrow, but the link to negotiated obligations is still maturing.
entries.reason:
This edge asks whether a contract can drive the movement of money: locking funds in escrow when an agreement is struck and releasing them on the agreed condition. Here the composition is relatively strong — escrow is a well-understood on-chain primitive, and delegation standards let contracts authorize payments, so the wiring between contracts and funds is genuinely workable.

It is graded emerging rather than higher because tying escrow conditions back to richly specified obligations, and ultimately to a verification verdict, is still early. Simple condition-based release works today; nuanced, obligation-aware escrow that reflects a negotiated agreement in full is still being built out. A capable link with clear room to deepen.

entries.name: Payment → Execution
entries.title: Paid work triggering execution
entries.summary: Payment can gate execution, but verifiable pay-for-work loops are largely ad hoc today.
entries.reason:
This integration covers whether a payment can reliably trigger and gate execution — the agent gets paid (or escrow is committed) and then performs the contracted work. The HTTP 402 pattern shows a tight version of this for per-request services, where payment and execution sit in the same call.

It is graded experimental because beyond simple per-request cases, the loop is mostly ad hoc. There is no standard way to bind an escrowed payment to a verifiable unit of executed work across different execution frameworks, so most implementations are custom. Payment and execution touch, but a dependable, interoperable pay-for-work handoff is not yet in place.

entries.name: Execution → Verification
entries.title: Executed work being verified
entries.summary: Verifying that executed work met the agreement is still mostly manual and framework-specific.
entries.reason:
This edge asks whether the result of executed work can be fed into verification — proving the deliverable matches the agreement so a verdict can be reached. Verification systems like oracles and AI juries can in principle ingest execution outputs and evidence, and the conceptual pipeline is well understood.

It is graded experimental because the practical link is weak. Execution frameworks rarely emit standardized, verifiable artifacts, so getting execution output into a verification system usually requires manual evidence assembly. Until execution produces verification-ready proofs by default, this remains one of the more fragile joints in the stack.

entries.name: Identity ↔ Verification (reputation loop)
entries.title: Verdicts feeding back into reputation
entries.summary: The loop from dispute verdicts back into agent reputation is conceptually clear but barely implemented.
entries.reason:
This connection closes the loop: the outcome of a verification or dispute should feed back into an agent's identity and reputation, so good and bad behavior accumulate over time. It is one of the most powerful ideas in the stack, because portable reputation is what makes discovery trustworthy in the first place.

It is graded experimental because the loop is largely aspirational today. Verification systems and identity registries are built by different teams with no shared standard for writing verdicts back as reputation signals. A few prototypes gesture at it, but in practice dispute outcomes rarely flow automatically into a counterparty's reputation. High-value, low-maturity.

entries.name: Contracts ↔ Verification (obligations judged)
entries.title: Contract obligations evaluated by a jury
entries.summary: Contract obligations can be expressed for an AI jury to judge, with real but early end-to-end examples.
entries.reason:
This edge is the heart of Internet Court: the obligations encoded in a contract become exactly what a verification system evaluates. GenLayer's intelligent contracts are designed for precisely this — a contract carries a statement, guidelines and evidence definitions, and the AI jury judges them — so there is a real, purpose-built path from contract to verdict.

It is graded emerging because, while the native integration exists and works, it is concentrated in one ecosystem and still early in production. Mapping arbitrary contract obligations from other standards into a judgeable form is not yet general, and high-volume autonomous use is just beginning. Where the contracts and verification layers share an engine this is strong; across heterogeneous standards it is still developing.

entries.name: Escrow ↔ Verification (resolution releases funds)
entries.title: Verdicts releasing escrowed funds
entries.summary: A verification verdict can release escrowed funds, with working patterns but limited cross-system standardization.
entries.reason:
This integration ensures the dispute outcome actually moves money: when verification returns a verdict, escrow releases to the rightful party. It is the mechanism that gives agent commerce teeth, and the pieces exist — escrow contracts can be conditioned on an oracle or jury result, and several systems demonstrate verdict-triggered settlement.

It is graded emerging because robust, standardized verdict-to-settlement flows are still maturing. Wiring a specific verification system to a specific escrow contract works, but there is no widely adopted, system-agnostic standard for it, so each integration is somewhat bespoke. The capability is real and improving, and it is one of the more important joints to harden for trustworthy agent commerce.
